overview: Charlemagne’s imperial coronation in 800 gave a new Roman title to a large Frankish monarchy. Its rulers joined conquest with Christian government and support for learning. The realm divided among his grandsons in 843; later Carolingian kings and emperors did not continuously govern one united empire. The map’s label through 1000 combines different political phases.

periods.title: Imperial court and contested succession
periods.summary: Charlemagne and Louis the Pious ruled an imperial realm. Disputes among Louis’s sons culminated in the partition of 843.

periods.title: Related kingdoms, intermittent unity
periods.summary: The western, eastern and middle kingdoms followed different paths. Charles the Fat briefly reunited much of the realm before his deposition in 887 and death in 888.

periods.title: A map label outlives unity
periods.summary: The imported label continues over later territories. Carolingian artistic and scholarly practices also survived changes of ruler.

sections.title: Court life, including the awkward bits

items.text: Einhard, a writer close to Charlemagne’s court, says the ruler enjoyed the warm baths at Aachen and invited sons, nobles and attendants to join him. The royal bath could be a social occasion. This describes a privileged court, not bathing facilities in every village.

According to Einhard, Charlemagne had his sons and daughters taught the liberal arts. Boys also practiced riding and hunting, while girls learned textile work. The account reveals a royal educational ideal with different expectations for boys and girls, rather than universal schooling.

Einhard says the aging ruler disliked doctors who urged him to exchange roasted meat for boiled meat. Even an emperor could be an uncooperative patient. The anecdote preserves a court writer’s portrait, not evidence that its dietary advice was effective medicine.

Charlemagne reportedly practiced writing on tablets kept beneath his pillow, but began late and made little progress. The same biography praises his interest in learned subjects. Being a powerful patron of books did not automatically make handwriting easy.

sections.title: What buildings, books and fields reveal

items.text: Aachen’s palace chapel organized worship around an eight-sided central space, with an upper gallery and a dome. Ancient columns were reused in the building. Its architecture connected the Carolingian court with prestigious Roman and Christian traditions through materials as well as ceremony.

The chapel’s surviving bronze gates belong to its early history, but the brilliant mosaic decorating today’s dome was installed in 1880 to 1881. A beautiful old building can contain several centuries at once. Archaeologists and architectural historians separate those layers before reconstructing Charlemagne’s surroundings.

Scholars such as Alcuin helped develop court learning and the copying of books. Carolingian minuscule used clearer, more regular letter forms that made manuscripts easier to read. This was a major scribal achievement, although producing a book still required skilled labor and expensive materials.

A Gospel book made around 825 to 850, probably at Metz, survives on parchment with ink and painted decoration. Its arcaded canon tables cross-reference passages in the four Gospels. They are both attractive pages and practical finding aids: a manuscript could help readers navigate as well as impress them.

The famous plan sent from Reichenau to St Gall around 820 consists of five pieces of parchment sewn together. It was prepared for Abbot Gozbert as a framework for thinking about a monastery. It is evidence for planning and ideals, not a photograph proving every building existed exactly as drawn.

The plan’s Latin dedicatory letter invites its readers to “perscrutinare,” meaning “examine closely,” and “sollertiam exercere,” meaning “exercise ingenuity.” These short phrases are transcribed in the abbey library’s scholarly catalogue. The designers expected the recipient to think about the plan, not simply copy it without judgment.

At Mérigest near modern Sénart, archaeologists identified a ninth-century rural unit with two timber-post buildings, a well and three successive cooking ovens. One building was probably a house. Successive ovens show replacement over time; they should not be imagined as three simultaneous kitchens in one family home.

Pits at the same site contained a millstone and iron objects including a cowbell, spur and key. Archaeologists suggest the metal may have been gathered for recycling. Grinding grain, managing animals and salvaging useful material become visible through objects whose owners’ names are lost.

Imperial expansion also involved coercion. A law issued during Charlemagne’s Saxon wars threatened death for refusing baptism. It shows rulers using severe penalties to impose Christianity. A legal threat is evidence of policy, however, not a record of how often a punishment was carried out.

ending.text: The partition of 843 created distinct kingdoms, though imperial titles and Carolingian dynasties continued. Charles the Fat’s later reunion collapsed in 887 to 888. The atlas’s 1000 endpoint is therefore not the fall of a continuously united empire.
